The Brachistochrone problem specifically investigates the curve of fastest descent. The name itself comes from the Greek words "brachistos" (shortest) and "chronos" (time), directly translating to "shortest time." The solution is a cycloid, not the straight line which represents the shortest distance.

A curved path (like a brachistochrone) allows the marble to drop more steeply at the beginning, converting potential energy to kinetic energy faster, leading to a higher average speed.

C
This is the classic "brachistochrone problem." The cycloid-shaped path allows the marble to gain speed most rapidly at the beginning due to its steep initial slope. This early acceleration results in a higher average speed over the entire course, making it the fastest path, even though it is not the shortest distance.

C
The Brachistochrone problem sought the path of fastest descent under gravity, and its solution was found to be an inverted cycloid. A cycloid is the curve traced by a point on the circumference of a wheel as it rolls along a straight line.

B
The steep initial descent rapidly converts gravitational potential energy into kinetic energy, allowing the object to build up a high velocity early on. This higher average speed over the entire path results in the shortest overall travel time, even though the path length is longer than a straight line.
